claim: Speakers' event descriptions show language-specific tendencies of differing consistency: English speakers used manner verbs in bounded events more than Greek speakers (72% vs 36%, 17 per group), and Swedish speakers used the satellite frame in 97% of caused-motion descriptions versus only 59% verb-framed in Spanish, where variation came mainly from the speaker.
agent_test: Not testable as LLM cognition; as a check, measure manner-verb rate when the same agent writes in two languages.
audit_note: Numbers verified (72% vs 36%; 97% vs 59%), but 'reliable' overstates: Montero-Melis's point is that Spanish descriptions are inconsistent (59% verb-framed, 35% satellite, variation mainly from the speaker), and the English/Greek result is 17 speakers per language.
claim_before_audit: Speakers' language-specific event descriptions are reliable: English speakers use manner verbs in bounded events more than Greek speakers (72% vs 36%), and Swedish speakers use one satellite frame 97% of the time vs 59% verb-framed in Spanish.

claim: While preparing to speak, gaze differs by language within the first second (Greek speakers look to the path endpoint first); this is the core thinking-for-speaking effect. Evidence is one lab, 17 per group, and item-level support is mixed (first-look interaction marginal by items).
agent_test: Compare agents that must answer in a fixed output format vs agents that plan freely: do the plan elements attended differ at equal tokens?

claim: Without a speaking task, eye movements and attention to motion events are nearly identical across English and Greek during the event (Papafragou 2008, Lee et al. 2026); differences appear after the event ends. CONTESTED by newer work: English vs French non-verbal categorisation differed (French 78% path-congruent vs English 59%, N=20 per language, Soroli 2024) and English vs Mandarin speakers differed in manner detection under flash suppression with no speaking (N=51-55 per group, Fu et al. 2023).
agent_test: If an agent encodes a problem silently first (no output format known), does its representation differ by output language? Compare probe accuracy.

claim: Language affects non-linguistic tasks only when language is used as a strategy during encoding: Papafragou 2008 found a Greek memory cost only in the nonlinguistic task; Gennari 2002 found a language-specific similarity effect only after verbal encoding and none in recognition memory.
agent_test: Add a describe-first step before a judgment task and measure whether the judgment shifts toward describe-language categories vs no describe step.

claim: Language differences in event segmentation are absent in non-linguistic tasks: English vs Turkish speakers differ strongly in multi-clause descriptions (beta=-3.84, N=39 vs 42) but not in non-linguistic event segmentation.
agent_test: None direct; supports keeping the representation step language-neutral.

claim: Counter-evidence: Korean vs German speakers' similarity ratings and gaze follow their own language's containment/support categories (N=27, partial eta2=.24), a language effect in a non-speaking task, although with explicit similarity ratings.
agent_test: Not applicable.

claim: Aspect and goal-mention differences between aspect and non-aspect languages, and bilingual switching of construal, exist but were seen only second-hand in this run.
agent_test: Not applicable.

claim: Attention drives sentence structure (gaze capture raises subject likelihood) and event structure feeds message planning; this is the production-model basis for the idea that early attention shapes what is said.
agent_test: Prime the agent plan with an entity (cue) and test whether the answer foregrounds it vs no cue.

claim: Goal bias is a language-independent attentional default in English speakers: Goal mentioned 97.7% vs Source 87.5%; fixation 1312 vs 913 ms; speaking shifts attention relatively toward Source.
agent_test: Check whether agent plans over-attend to end states (goals) and under-attend to sources/preconditions; add a checklist and compare.

claim: Reasoning LLMs think mostly in English whatever the input language, and forcing reasoning in the input language lowers accuracy (MATH-500 Swahili 57.4 to 25.9; Spanish 88.0 to 72.5; XReasoning prompt hack raised matching from 46% to 98% and cut mean accuracy from 26% to 17%, with AIME 25.5 to 17.0 for Distill-R1-32B). Three independent groups agree on the trade-off. Language-consistency RL (M-Thinker) reaches nearly 100% consistency with reported gains on MMATH and PolyMath, suggesting the problem may be fixable in training, though the paper's abstract does not show the accuracy cost vanishes.
agent_test: Run the same tasks with reasoning forced to English vs the input language at equal tokens.
audit_note: Numbers and the three-group trade-off check out (Tam et al., Qi et al., Zhao et al.), but M-Thinker's abstract only reports near-100% consistency and 'superior performance' on MMATH/PolyMath; it does not show the accuracy cost disappears, so 'the cost belongs to current models and not to the language itself' is an unsupported inference.
claim_before_audit: Reasoning LLMs think mostly in English whatever the input language, and forcing reasoning in the input language lowers accuracy (MATH-500 Swahili 57.4 to 25.9; Spanish 88.0 to 72.5; XReasoning prompt hack raised matching from 46% to 98% and cut mean accuracy 26% to 17%, with AIME 25.5 to 17.0 for Distill-R1-32B). Three independent groups agree on the trade-off. Language-consistency RL (M-Thinker) restores near 100% consistency, so the cost belongs to current models and not to the language itself.

claim: Latent concept representation in middle layers is English-biased: logit lens shows English-close tokens even in non-English output (Llama-2 and Llama-3.1-70B), though Wendler et al. find a language-neutral concept and Schut et al. find an English route; the training mix changes the latent language (Japanese models).
agent_test: Not testable at scaffold level; background.

claim: Self-translating the input to English before answering helps multilingual models: +3.5 mean accuracy for LLaMA 30B (43.1 to 46.6), XNLI 37.0 to 43.5, MGSM flat (15.5 to 16.3); gains grow with model size.
agent_test: Compare direct answering vs translate-then-answer on a non-English subset; count tokens.

claim: Chain-of-thought works across languages without large cost: PaLM-540B average of 4 underrepresented languages 44.9% vs 47.9% over 6 high-resource languages; translate-to-English gave similar results.
agent_test: None.

claim: The language the model thinks in changes the diversity of its output: non-English thinking raises NoveltyBench Distinct Score by 5.3 to 7.7 points over English (Qwen3-8B 28.55 vs 36.00; mixed 43.73), with output quality drop 1.02 to 2.24; r=0.72-0.88 with distance from English.
agent_test: Test diversity of candidate generation when branches are reasoned in different languages at equal total tokens. Closest LLM analogue of this subfield.

claim: Language-specific causal-order preferences exist in models (BICAUSE, Qwen1.5-1.8B reversed chains English 88.5 vs Chinese 76.5), but the gap shrinks with scale (14B 97.5 both) and direction differs by model family; so this is weak evidence.
agent_test: Not worth testing in the scaffold.

claim: LLM colour naming tracks human naming in English and in Russian prompts (GPT-4 agreement 0.59 vs 0.54), and text-only models align with perceptual colour space; so statistics of language alone carry some perceptual structure.
agent_test: None; background on what language-only systems encode.
audit_note: Agreement is an adjusted Rand index well below the human ceiling (0.73-0.75), and GPT-4 may have had non-text training, so the Marjieh result alone does not isolate language statistics; Abdou et al.'s BERT-family result supports the text-only point.

claim: No study was found that gives an LLM motion-event stimuli and measures manner/path encoding by language (Slobin paradigm); the nearest is a Latin motion annotation test (GPT-4 Goal F1 about 0.82; small Llama over-labels Goal, precision 0.19-0.26). This is an open gap, not a confirmed absence.
agent_test: Build a small Slobin-style test: describe motion events in English vs Greek/Spanish/Turkish and measure manner omission.

claim: Several LLM papers share the name 'thinking while speaking' / 'think before speak' but are architecture papers and do not test Slobin's claim; Quiet-STaR (GSM8K 5.9 to 10.9; CommonsenseQA 36.3 to 47.2) is internal rationale before output.
agent_test: Treat as name overlap only; the agent-level analogue is a private plan step before the final answer, already covered by schema states.
audit_note: 'Do not test Slobin's claim' is an absence claim; Quiet-STaR (GSM8K 5.9 to 10.9, CSQA 36.3 to 47.2) and the two name-overlap papers verified from abstracts only.

claim: Multi-language sampling plus voting can beat a matched single-language control on correctness: UL-XCoT 83.8 vs UL-CoT 65.5 on PolyMath-Low, 31.1 vs 26.3 Medium, 13.6 vs 12.3 High, 10.6 vs 9.4 Top (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, 18 languages), with over 50% fewer decoding tokens than prior sampling baselines. In one Qwen2.5-7B test a non-English response language beat English for some questions (zh 87.2 vs en 81.2 on English MGSM questions; average zh 65.09 vs en 64.22). Not shown at strictly equal tokens and not on frontier models.
agent_test: Branch generation with forced different reasoning languages vs same-language branches at equal total tokens on 100 items from MATH-500 and GPQA; log both correctness and candidate diversity.

claim: Language-specific effects in event tasks grow with how much language is involved. Soroli 2024: English vs French verbal similarity gap (M 67% vs 41%) was larger than the non-verbal one (M 41% vs 22%). Fu et al. 2023: the same manner/path contrast gave opposite RT patterns in a detection task and in a sentence-video verification task. Athanasopoulos & Bylund (second-hand): aspect differences vanished under verbal interference.
agent_test: Compare accuracy of a judgment step after a label-priming step vs after a distractor step, at equal tokens.

claim: Verbal reasoning before a perceptual or implicit judgement can hurt models as it hurts people: GPT-4o 64.0% to 51.2% and Claude 3 Opus 44.0% to 29.6% on face recognition after description; artificial grammar 94.0% (GPT-4o) vs 57.7% (o1-preview); GPT-4o 87.5% to 64.4% with CoT. Three tasks that hurt humans do not hurt models, so the parallel is partial. This is indirect evidence on gap 5 and not a Gennari-type test.
agent_test: Add a describe-first step before pattern or similarity judgements; compare accuracy against no describe step at equal tokens.

claim: The Wendler (language-neutral concept, single token) vs Schut (English route for content words, multi-token open generation) disagreement is partly explained by task design and model: the authors of the second paper name the single-token vs multi-token contrast, and English-centrism varies by model (Aya-23-35B least, Gemma-2-27b most). Reasoning-trained models were not tested in either paper.
agent_test: Not a scaffold test; background.

claim: Page-level reading of Slobin's evidence is still second-hand: per Gennari et al. 2002, Slobin 1996-1998 used Spanish-English translations, narrations of the same pictures and mental images, and every response pattern was linguistic; the cognitive claim (habitual attention to manner for Manner-language speakers) is a hypothesis for thinking-for-speaking. Slobin 1996 and Berman & Slobin 1994 frog-story numbers by language and age were not obtained.
agent_test: Not applicable.

claim: No large (over 100 per group) or preregistered replication of the Papafragou 2008 gaze-timing result was found. Related work uses 20 per cell (Soroli 2024) or about 50 per group (Fu et al. 2023) and different paradigms.
agent_test: Not applicable.
